title: The five, the four, the forty
hook: it remembers the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty liberated

segments.voice: Yesterday: jot, and your line: the ten in one. Did a candle or a lamp remind you of the flame? Now the Ardas turns from the Gurus to the Sikhs who stood with them. Day six hundred twenty-one.

Three numbers. Say them fast and they sound like a phone number: five, four, forty. Each number is a group of people. One group stepped forward when everyone else stepped back. One group was four brothers, two of them still small boys. One group walked away from their Guru, and then came back. The Ardas says all three numbers in a single breath, right after the Guru Granth Sahib, before any other Sikhs it remembers. Today: the five, the four, the forty.
screen: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.` → `THREE GROUPS OF PEOPLE.` → `SAID IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The line goes: panjaan piaariaan, chauhaan sahibzaadiaan, chaaleeaan mukteaan. The five beloved, the four princes, the forty liberated. The five: the Panj Pyare. At Vaisakhi at Anandpur, Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh stood before a huge gathering with a sword and asked for someone willing to give their head. A long silence. Then one man stood. Then four more. As the story is told, they came from different castes and regions: a shopkeeper, a farmer, a water carrier, a washerman, a barber. They were the first initiated into the Khalsa, and Sikhs say the Guru then asked them to initiate him. Ever since, five initiated Sikhs lead the amrit ceremony. The four: the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. The two older ones, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, died fighting at Chamkaur. The two younger ones, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, still small boys, were captured and executed at Sirhind after, tradition says, refusing to give up their faith. Sikhs mark their martyrdom every year. The forty: the Chali Mukte. During the siege of Anandpur, a group of Sikhs left the Guru and, tradition says, signed a paper disowning him. At home, they were shamed for it, and a woman named Mai Bhago led them back. They fought at Khidrana, now Muktsar, and fell. As the last of them was dying, the story goes, the Guru tore up the paper. That's why they're called mukte, the liberated. Five who stepped forward. Four who held on. Forty who came back. Sikhs hear in them three ways a person can be faithful.
screen: `THE FIVE: WHO STOOD UP.` · `THE FOUR: THE GURU'S SONS.` · `THE FORTY: WHO CAME BACK.` · `THREE WAYS TO BE FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say five, four, forty. Sit and breathe. On one out-breath, say: five, and picture people standing up in a silent crowd. On the next: four, and picture four brothers, two grown and two small. On the next: forty, and picture people walking back toward someone they'd left. Repeat it slowly. Notice which of the three you understand best right now: stepping forward, holding on, or coming back. If you pray, you can follow with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The five. The Panj Pyare who stood up, the four Sahibzade, and the forty who came back: remembered in one breath.
Your line: five, four, forty. If there's someone you've drifted from, take one small step back toward them today. Day six hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty Muktas in one line; five initiated Sikhs still lead every amrit ceremony, and the Sahibzade's martyrdom is marked each year.

fork.setup: Vaisakhi at Anandpur. the Guru stands with a sword and asks for someone willing to give their head. the crowd is silent. what does tradition say happened?
options: nobody answered and he put the sword away.
one man stood, then four more.
the whole crowd stood at once.
fork.reveal: one by one, five stood. they became the Panj Pyare, the first of the Khalsa, and Sikhs say the Guru then asked them to initiate him.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, first initiated into the Khalsa.

trapdoor: what you thought: five, four, forty is a list of numbers to memorize.
what it means: three groups who show three ways to be faithful: stepping forward, holding on, coming back.
what a scholar hears: the Ardas reads panjaan piaariaan, chauhaan sahibzaadiaan, chaaleeaan mukteaan; tradition says Khidrana was renamed Muktsar after the forty.

sources.ref: Ardas, as set out in the Sikh Rehat Maryada (SGPC)

notes: Occupations of the Panj Pyare (shopkeeper, farmer, water carrier, washerman, barber) as commonly told: confirm.
Sahibzade dates and ages (Chamkaur December 1704; Zorawar Singh about nine, Fateh Singh about six, at Sirhind): some sources give 1705; confirm.
Story of the bedava (disclaimer) torn up for Mahan Singh at Khidrana: traditional; confirm.
Oldest Sahibzada 'about eighteen' (Ajit Singh, born 1687): confirm.
